articles.title: Trump Whisperer Shares Bonkers AI Video to Defend Plane Swap
articles.description: Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Imag MAGA activist Laura Loomer shared a bizarre AI-generated fantasy to defend the president’s plane swap. Loomer, 33, shared the unhinged video on X in defense of the president following a bombshell report from the Washington Post that detailed a secret plane transfer to protect President Donald Trump from an Iranian assassination threat last month. The AI-generated video shared by Loomer, a staunch defender of the war in Iran, depicts President Donald Trump and what appears to be dozens of journalists boarding the Qatari-donated Air Force One to the theme of the Mission: Impossible soundtrack. Read more at The Daily Beast.

articles.title: "I think that might be a misread": Thief designer on why making a triple-A immersive sim doesn't really work
articles.description: Broadly speaking, it's fine for something to exist as a niche. Whatever form of media a thing might be, to fulfil a niche is to meet the expectations of at least a handful of people with a particular taste that many others don't, and I think that's a delightful thing to do. In video games, immersive sims might not be the most niche genre in the world, but they've historically not done gangbusters sales wise, meaning that triple-A takes don't quite make their money back. If you ask Randy Smith Evergreen, a designer on Thief: The Dark Project , perhaps avoiding the world of triple-A is the way to go for immersive sims. Read more

articles.title: Flight paths and fridge magnets: how a fireball hunter tracked down New Zealand’s newest meteorite
articles.description: A network of cameras helped guide a group of space enthusiasts to New Zealand’s 11th confirmed meteorite Days after a massive fireball flashed through New Zealand’s skies last month , Steve Wyn-Harris spotted a small, black stone on the bare ground. The citizen astronomer was on the hunt for debris from the meteor that had flown over the North Island. He bagged the rock but wasn’t too confident, as he says most finds turn out to be “meteor-wrongs”. But when he held the thumb-sized rock next to a fridge magnet, to detect iron and nickel in meteorites, it clicked. Wyn-Harris did the test on a video call with other citizen scientists and geologists and after the click “we were all yelling”. Continue reading...
